Today’s failing approach: technical interview outsourcing followed by a second round
Buyers report $250 to $350 per outsourced technical interview, billed whether it ends in an offer or a rejection.
Your hiring manager wasn’t in the room, so they book their own session to be sure. Most teams now call that a filter and budget for both.
The vendor owns the questions. The session tests their library, not your stack.
Candidates meet a stranger, and senior engineers warn each other off the format in public.
That’s two paid conversations before anyone makes a decision.
Keep the structure, drop the middleman
Codility Interview is a shared VS Code workspace your own engineers run. The tasks come from Codility’s validated library, or you bring your own. Your team sets the rubric, and every session ends with rubric scores, a transcript, playback and reviewable AI activity.
Codility Screen takes the shortlisting, your engineers take the interview
Today you run three stages: your screen, the provider’s interview, then the hiring manager round that happens anyway.
Codility Screen takes over the shortlisting the provider’s round does today, using role-relevant engineering tasks.
Your engineers run the technical interview in Codility Interview, with the candidates on the Screen shortlist. Your team does not spend interview time on candidates who do not fit the role.
The separate outsourced round comes out of your process.
One session, one record, nothing left to schedule.

Your engineers interview where they work
The session runs in shared VS Code, with a terminal, package installs, autocomplete and the AI Copilot. Your engineers see the candidate work with AI, the way they would on the job.
Whiteboard and system design happen in the same window, so architecture and code are not split across two tools.
Your engineers run the session on tasks from Codility’s validated library or on their own, and score against one rubric your team sets.
You watch someone work on a Monday, and they meet the team they’d join.
The record is ready when the session ends
Rubric scores, a full transcript, step-by-step playback and the AI activity log are there the moment the interview finishes.
Nobody chases an engineer for a scorecard.
And when a hiring committee reopens the decision six months later, they can see how it was reached rather than take somebody’s word for it.
Feedback in minutes, evidence that survives an audit.

When technical interview as a service is still the better buy
Some teams should keep it. If your engineers truly can’t give up the hours, or you hire in two short bursts a year, or nobody internally will own the rubric, a vendor that supplies interviewers earns its money. Codility Interview is for teams who’d rather run the round themselves and want it structured and recorded when they do.

Questions buyers ask
A vendor supplies trained interviewers who run your first-round technical interviews and sends back a scorecard with a recommendation. Most buyers keep it as a filter and run their own round afterward, which is where the second cost shows up.
Billed per interview, and buyers report $250 to $350 a session
The interviewer isn’t on your team and doesn’t use your tasks
The promise is engineering hours returned
Three, realistically. Codility Interview is the third one.
Keep the service and accept the per-interview cost
Go back to ad hoc technical interviews on a video call and a shared document, which is cheap and leaves you nothing to review
Run the round on a platform your engineers already work in, which produces a rubric score, a transcript and playback from every session
Yes, and most teams treat it as a deliberate filter rather than a mistake. Worth asking whether the filter needs to be a separate paid round, when one structured session your own team runs can do both jobs.
